PageRank Using a Markov Chain Model
Implementation on a simulated web graph
and analysis of the damping factor
Foundations of Data Science • Assessment 7

1. Simulated Web Graph & Markov Model
Eight webpages are represented as states in a directed graph.
• 8 webpages (A–H) with 14 directed hyperlinks.
• Webpages are states; hyperlinks are possible transitions.
• The adjacency matrix is converted into a probability 
transition matrix P .
• Each row of P sums to 1, forming a Markov transition 
matrix.
• Page H is a dangling node and is assigned a uniform 
transition distribution.

2. PageRank as a Markov Chain
Power iteration finds the stationary probability distribution.
• Initialize the PageRank vector uniformly: r₀ = [1/N, …, 
1/N].
• Use the damping factor α to combine link-following and 
teleportation.
• Google matrix: G = αP + (1−α)E.
• Iterate: rₜ₊₁ = rₜG until the change is below the 
tolerance.
• PageRank is a probability distribution, so the scores sum 
to 1.
G = αP + (1−α)E
rₜ₊₁ = rₜG
Σ PageRank = 1

3. Impact of the Damping Factor
Experiment: α = 0.50, 0.70, 0.85, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99.
• Lower α means more teleportation and 
a more uniform distribution.
• Higher α makes rankings more 
dependent on hyperlink structure.
• Page C rises from 0.1920 at α=0.50 to 
0.2602 at α=0.99.
• Page H falls from 0.0925 to 0.0403.
• Convergence takes 20, 29, 39, 43, 48 
and 53 iterations respectively.

4. Results, Validation & Conclusion
• At α = 0.85, Page C has the highest PageRank: ≈ 0.2399.
• Page E is second with ≈ 0.2275.
• The custom implementation was validated against NetworkX.
• Maximum absolute difference: ≈ 1.15 × 10⁻¹⁰.
• PageRank can be interpreted as the stationary distribution of a 
Markov chain.
• The damping factor controls both ranking behaviour and 
convergence.
